title: Pure Functions & Immutability
summary: The two disciplines all of functional programming is built on: a pure function's output depends only on its input, and immutable data never changes under you. Together they make code predictable and concurrency safe by construction.

slides.markdown:
Two rules underpin functional programming, and almost everything else in this group is a consequence of them: a **pure function** always returns the same output for the same input and touches nothing outside itself, and **immutable data** never changes after it's created.

Neither rule is exotic. You already write pure functions — `Math.max(a, b)` is one. The shift is treating purity as the *default* for your own code, not the exception.

The payoff shows up everywhere else you'll study in this area: it's why closures are safe to share, why concurrency gets easier, and why a function is trivial to unit test. This topic is the foundation the rest stands on.

slides.subTitle: Two conditions, both required
slides.markdown:
A function is **pure** when both hold:

1. **Deterministic output** — given the same arguments, it always returns the same result. No hidden dependency on the clock, a random source, a global counter, or a database row that might have changed.
2. **No observable side effects** — it doesn't mutate an argument, write to a variable outside its scope, print, log, throw for control flow, or touch the filesystem/network.

`add(2, 3)` is pure: same in, same out, forever. `Date.now()` is impure — same call, different answer every time. `deposit(account, amount)` that mutates `account.balance` is impure even though it looks deterministic, because it has a side effect.

Both conditions matter independently: a function can be deterministic and still impure (it mutates something), or side-effect-free and still impure (it reads a mutable global, so the *same* call can answer differently later).

slides.subTitle: Swap the call for its result — nothing changes
slides.markdown:
**Referential transparency** is the practical superpower purity buys you: any call to a pure function can be replaced by the value it returns, anywhere in the program, without changing what the program does.

If `square(4)` is pure, you can substitute `16` for `square(4)` everywhere it appears and the program behaves identically. That's what lets a compiler **memoize** a pure function's results, evaluate it lazily, or run several calls in parallel and merge the results — all without asking the programmer's permission, because reordering or repeating the call can't change the outcome.

An impure call can't be substituted this way. Replace `logAndIncrement()` with its return value and you silently delete a side effect the rest of the program was relying on. Referential transparency is the property optimizers, memoizers, and parallelizers all depend on — it's why "is this pure?" is the first question a compiler-level optimization has to answer.

slides.sectionTitle: A pure function has no hidden wires
slides.markdown:
The mental model that makes purity easy to spot: draw the function as a box. A pure function has exactly one kind of arrow going in (its parameters) and exactly one kind coming out (its return value) — nothing else crosses the boundary.

An impure function has extra, invisible wires: a read from a global or captured mutable variable sneaking in, or a mutation/print/network call sneaking out. Those hidden wires are exactly what makes the function hard to reason about — you can't tell what it does by reading its signature.

slides.sectionTitle: Mutating in place vs. returning new
slides.markdown:
The same operation — appending a discount to every price — written the impure way and the pure way:

```python
# Impure: mutates the caller's list, returns nothing
def apply_discount(prices, pct):
    for i in range(len(prices)):
        prices[i] = prices[i] * (1 - pct)
    # caller's original list is gone

# Pure: leaves the input untouched, returns a new list
def apply_discount_pure(prices, pct):
    return [p * (1 - pct) for p in prices]
```

Call `apply_discount(cart, 0.1)` and every other part of the program still holding a reference to `cart` now sees discounted prices — even code that never asked for a discount. Call `apply_discount_pure(cart, 0.1)` and `cart` is exactly as it was; you get a new list back and decide whether to use it.

The pure version costs an allocation. In exchange, nothing else in the program can be surprised by this call.

A **race condition** requires two things at once: shared state, and at least one writer. Remove either one and the race is impossible — immutability removes the writer.

If a value can never change after creation, two threads reading it simultaneously can never observe it half-updated, and there's nothing to lock. Clojure's persistent data structures and Erlang/Elixir's actor model both lean on this: pass immutable messages between processes and you've deleted an entire category of bugs (torn reads, lost updates, deadlocks from lock ordering) without writing a single mutex.

Compare that to a shared mutable counter incremented from multiple threads: every read-modify-write needs a lock or an atomic instruction, and forgetting one produces a bug that only shows up under load, non-deterministically, in production. Immutability doesn't make concurrency free — coordinating *which* new value wins is still a real problem — but it deletes the "who's mutating this right now" class of bug entirely.

slides.subTitle: Sharing structure instead of deep-copying
slides.markdown:
If "immutable" meant "deep-copy on every change," functional programs would be too slow to use — updating one element of a million-item list would copy a million items. **Persistent data structures** avoid this by sharing almost all of the old structure with the new one.

The classic example is a persistent tree: appending an element rebuilds only the **path from the root to the changed node** — typically O(log n) nodes — and every other branch is shared, by reference, between the old and new versions. Both versions are fully valid and usable afterward; nothing was mutated, so the old one didn't stop existing.

This is exactly how Clojure's vectors and maps, and Scala's `List`/`Vector`, give you "copy on every update" semantics at a cost close to a mutable structure's, rather than an actual full copy's O(n) cost.

The failure mode that trips up code review: a function that *looks* pure — no obvious mutation of its arguments — but isn't, because of something outside the signature.

- **Secretly logs or metrics.** `def total(items): log.info(f"summing {len(items)}"); return sum(items)` — deterministic output, but it has a side effect (writing to a log stream), so it isn't pure. Harmless in isolation, but it means the function can't be freely memoized or reordered without changing what gets logged.
- **Mutates a captured variable.** A closure that increments an outer counter every time it's called returns a value that *looks* like a pure computation but changes behavior across calls.
- **Throws for control flow.** A function that raises an exception on some inputs instead of returning a value (like `Result`/`Option`) has a side channel in its control flow that referential transparency doesn't cover — you can't safely "replace the call with its result" if the call might not return at all.

The test that catches all three: call the function twice with identical arguments, in either order, and diff *everything* observable — return value, logs, global state, exceptions raised. Purity means that diff is empty.

slides.sectionTitle: Imperative vs. functional update, side by side
slides.markdown:
Same task — remove completed items from a to-do list — two styles:

| | Imperative (mutate in place) | Functional (return new) |
|---|---|---|
| Code shape | `for`/`while` loop with index bookkeeping, often removing while iterating | one `filter` expression |
| Aliasing risk | any other reference to the list sees the change immediately | zero — old list is untouched |
| Testability | must assert on the mutated list after the call | assert directly on the return value |
| Undo | requires you to have kept a manual copy beforehand | trivial — the old list still exists |
| Typical cost | O(n) time, O(1) extra space | O(n) time, O(n) extra space (new list) |

Neither is universally "better" — the imperative version is cheaper in memory, which matters in a tight loop over millions of elements. The functional version trades that memory for safety: nothing else in the program can be surprised by the change, and the old version stays around for free.

Testing an impure function usually means testing an *environment*: mocking the clock, stubbing the database, spinning up a fake filesystem, then asserting on side effects that happened somewhere else. Testing a pure function means calling it and asserting on the return value — no setup, no mocks, no teardown.

This is also why pure functions are the natural target for **[property-based testing](property-based-and-specialized-testing)**: since a pure function's behavior is fully described by input → output, a testing library can throw thousands of generated inputs at it and check invariants (`reverse(reverse(xs)) == xs`) instead of you hand-writing individual cases.

The practical interview signal: when you're asked "why is this function hard to unit test," the answer is almost always "it depends on something outside its arguments, or changes something outside its return value" — and the fix is to pull that dependency out as a parameter and push the side effect out to the caller, i.e., make the core logic pure and push impurity to the edges.
